name: Poker tells

card.summary: Poker tells are involuntary behavioural cues that reveal a player's hand, and the same cue-reading framework is used in looksmaxxing circles to think about how posture, expression and demeanour shape the impression a person gives.
card.note: Borrowed from card games; community use for appearance is informal and no studies test it for looks.

quick.overview:
A tell, in poker, is a change in a player's behaviour or demeanour that some believe reveals how strong their hand is. Reading a tell correctly gives an edge, and players also try to suppress their own or fake tells to mislead opponents. The idea matters to looks because the cues in question, such as posture, facial expression, gaze and the way someone handles objects, are part of how a person comes across.

The best-known popular treatment is Mike Caro's Book of Tells (1994). The wider literature on tells is mostly practitioner guidance rather than controlled research, and Wikipedia notes that many specific rules of thumb are unsourced.
quick.how: In practice, people study the observable categories poker writers describe: body position, breathing, voice tone, facial expression, eye contact, and the handling of cards, chips or drinks. Those who borrow the framework for self-presentation use it as a checklist of what their own demeanour might signal, for example steady gaze and relaxed posture versus fidgeting or stiffness.
quick.risks: No physical risk is involved. The main caveat discussed by writers on the topic is reliability: a cue only tells something if the observer reads it accurately, and clumsiness or habit can create false tells.

lead: A tell in poker is a change in a player's behaviour or demeanour that is believed to reveal how the player rates their hand. Observing and correctly interpreting a reliable, unconscious tell is said to give an advantage, while players may also feign tells to mislead opponents [1].

In looksmaxxing discussion the concept is used as shorthand for the involuntary signals people give off through posture, facial expression, gaze and mannerisms. Because these cues are part of how a person is perceived, practitioners of self-presentation treat awareness of them as a way to come across more confident or composed, a chain that runs from noticing one's own cues to adjusting demeanour to a better impression.
The classic popular reference is Mike Caro's Book of Tells, published in 1994 [1]. Most writing on tells is practitioner experience rather than experimental study.

chain: Notice involuntary cues such as posture, gaze and fidgeting
Adjust or suppress cues that give a different impression than intended
Come across as more composed and confident
angle.text: People who borrow the poker framework use it as a checklist for self-presentation: what the body and face signal when they are not thinking about it. The payoff proponents describe is a steadier, more confident impression.

paras: Wikipedia describes tells as physical or behavioural changes believed to reveal a player's assessment of their hand. Physical examples include leaning forward or back, how forcefully chips are placed, fidgeting, nervous tics, breathing, tone of voice, facial expressions and gaze [1]. Handling of cards, chips, cigarettes or drinks is another category, and online play adds cues such as speed of play, betting patterns and chat [1].
A tell may be common to a class of players or unique to one individual [1]. Many players try to avoid giving tells by maintaining a neutral 'poker face', and some deliberately fake tells [1].

One widely repeated rule of thumb is 'weak means strong, strong means weak': a player holding a poor hand may act intimidating, while one holding a strong hand may appear passive or friendly to encourage calls [1]. Wikipedia flags this and other claims on the page as lacking citations [1].
Writers also caution that clumsy behaviour such as dropped chips, wrong bets or misclicks online can produce false tells unrelated to hand strength [1].

In appearance-focused communities, the term is used loosely for any unconscious signal that shapes first impressions, including posture, resting facial expression, eye contact and fidgeting. The reading goes both ways: learning to notice others' cues, and learning what one's own body is communicating. Proponents describe it as part of the behavioural side of presentation alongside grooming and clothing.
No studies found. Research on nonverbal behaviour and deception detection exists as a broader field, but no clinical study has tested poker tells as a method for improving appearance.

timeline.event: Mike Caro's Book of Tells is published by Carol Publishing Corporation [1].
